title: The Strategy Engine
tagline: Where the book becomes a decision — event-driven, deterministic, and fast enough to act before the edge evaporates.

concept.analogy: The strategy engine is the driver of a race car who only gets to act on what the dashboard shows right now. Every time the dashboard updates (a market event), the driver instantly decides: accelerate, brake, or hold. The decision logic must be rehearsed and reflexive — there's no time to 'think' from scratch. The car (OMS) and the safety system (risk) carry out and constrain the driver's commands, but the split-second judgment lives here.
paragraphs: The strategy engine sits between the order book and the OMS. It is event-driven: on each relevant market event (book update, trade, your own fill, a timer) it runs a callback that reads current state, computes a decision, and emits actions — place, cancel, or modify orders. The art of HFT software is making that callback both smart (captures the alpha) and fast/deterministic (executes in nanoseconds with low jitter) — two goals that constantly pull against each other.

The crucial split is between research and execution. Heavy modeling — fitting signals, calibrating parameters, training models — happens offline or on a side thread. The hot-path strategy code is the distilled result: a small, branch-predictable computation over precomputed parameters (e.g., compute microprice and imbalance, compare to thresholds, decide quotes). You never run a regression or allocate on the hot path; you evaluate a compact decision rule whose inputs were prepared elsewhere.

Determinism matters for correctness as well as speed. A good engine processes events in a single, well-defined order (one thread, no shared mutable state races), which makes behavior reproducible — essential for debugging and for backtests that match live trading. Many engines are built so the same strategy code runs unchanged over historical data (backtest), simulated data (paper), and live feeds, with only the event source and the order gateway swapped. That symmetry is a major architectural win: what you tested is what you run.

State management is the other half. The engine tracks its own resting orders and queue positions, current inventory/position, working PnL, and per-event timers, updating them as fills and cancels come back. It must react not just to the market but to its own order lifecycle (acks, fills, rejects). Keeping this state compact, cache-resident, and updated in O(1) — and reacting correctly to out-of-order or rejected messages — is what separates a robust engine from a fragile one.
points: Event-driven: each market/own-order event runs a fast callback that reads state and emits place/cancel/modify actions.
Split research (offline/side-thread modeling) from execution (a compact, branch-predictable hot-path rule over precomputed params).
Determinism: single ordered event processing → reproducible behavior; same code for backtest, paper, and live.
Manage own state: resting orders, queue position, inventory, PnL — updated O(1) on fills/cancels/rejects.
React to your own order lifecycle (acks/fills/rejects), not just the market.

callouts.title: One event loop, one source of truth
callouts.body: Run the strategy on a single thread processing a single ordered event stream (market + own-order events merged). No locks, no shared-state races, fully reproducible — and trivially fast because there's no synchronization on the hot path.

callouts.title: Don't put research in the hot path
callouts.body: Fitting, optimization, and model inference belong offline or on a side thread that hands parameters in. The hot callback should be a few comparisons and arithmetic ops, not a solver.

concept.keyIdea: The strategy engine is a single-threaded, event-driven loop that turns each market/own-order event into a fast, branch-predictable decision over precomputed parameters, while maintaining compact O(1) state (orders, queue position, inventory, PnL). Separating offline research from hot-path execution — and running the same code in backtest, paper, and live — gives both alpha and determinism.

deepDive.intro: The event loop, the research/execution split, deterministic state, and the backtest-equals-live design.

steps.title: The event loop and callbacks
steps.detail: The engine consumes a merged, time-ordered stream of events: market-data updates (from the book), own-order events (ack/fill/cancel/reject), and timers. Each dispatches to a handler (onBookUpdate, onFill, onTimer) that reads state and may emit actions. Handlers are small and must not block, allocate, or lock — they compute and enqueue order actions to the OMS via a lock-free ring.

steps.title: Research vs execution boundary
steps.detail: Define a narrow parameter interface: the research process produces a compact ParamSet (thresholds, coefficients, sizes, skew), updated infrequently (and atomically swapped in). The hot path reads ParamSet and current book state and applies a fixed decision rule. This keeps the hot path tiny and lets researchers iterate models without touching latency-critical code.

steps.title: Deterministic state
steps.detail: Hold strategy state in plain, cache-resident structs: a map/array of your working orders (by exchange/client id) with their level and queue position, current inventory and average price, realized/unrealized PnL, and timers. Update it O(1) on each event. Single-threaded processing means no data races and exactly-reproducible behavior given the same event sequence — invaluable for debugging and replay.

steps.title: Reacting to your own orders
steps.detail: Half the events are your own: an ack confirms a resting order (update queue estimate), a fill changes inventory/PnL and may trigger a hedge or re-quote, a reject means re-evaluate (maybe risk or exchange rejected it), a cancel-ack frees state. Handle partial fills, out-of-order acks, and races (a fill arriving before the ack) carefully — these edge cases are where real bugs live.

steps.title: Backtest = paper = live
steps.detail: Architect so the strategy depends only on abstract interfaces: an event source and an order interface. Swap the source (historical file / simulator / live feed) and the order sink (sim matcher / paper / live gateway) without changing strategy code. Then your backtest exercises the exact production logic, dramatically reducing 'works in backtest, breaks live' surprises (model fills realistically — see the backtesting lesson).

notes.title: Re-quote by diffing
notes.detail: Don't cancel-and-replace every event; compute the desired quotes and only send the orders that changed (or use modify) to minimize message traffic and preserve queue priority where possible.

notes.title: Parameter swaps must be safe
notes.detail: Update params via an atomic pointer/double-buffer so the hot path always reads a consistent ParamSet without locking; never mutate the live set field-by-field.

notes.title: Time is an input
notes.detail: Many strategies act on timers (refresh quotes, age out signals). Drive timers from the same event clock so backtest and live behave identically.

complexity.timeReason: Each callback is a small fixed computation over cache-resident state plus an O(1) state update; no allocation, locks, or model fitting on the path.
complexity.spaceReason: Compact structs for resting orders, inventory, PnL, and parameters — pre-allocated and cache-resident.

pitfalls: Running model fitting/inference or allocating on the hot callback instead of using precomputed parameters.
Multi-threaded shared mutable strategy state → races and non-reproducible behavior.
Ignoring own-order edge cases (partial fills, fill-before-ack, rejects) — the source of most live bugs.
Cancel/replace on every tick, flooding the exchange and losing queue priority unnecessarily.
Backtest and live using different code paths, so tested behavior ≠ live behavior.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you keep a strategy both 'smart' (good signals) and fast/deterministic on the hot path?
a: Separate research from execution. The heavy thinking — fitting signals, calibrating thresholds, training models — happens offline or on a non-critical side thread and produces a compact parameter set (coefficients, thresholds, sizes, skew). The hot-path callback just reads those precomputed parameters plus current book state and applies a small, branch-predictable decision rule (e.g., compute microprice/imbalance, compare to thresholds, decide quotes), emitting order actions over a lock-free ring. No fitting, no allocation, no locks on the path.

Determinism comes from running the strategy single-threaded over a single ordered event stream, so there are no data races and behavior is reproducible. Parameters are swapped in atomically (double-buffer) so the hot path never sees a torn update. This gives you alpha (from the research that shaped the parameters) without sacrificing nanosecond, low-jitter execution.

interviewQuestions.q: Why do firms architect the strategy so the same code runs in backtest, paper, and live? How?
a: Because the biggest risk is 'it worked in backtest but behaves differently live.' If the live and backtest logic are different code, your tests don't actually validate what you run. Sharing one strategy implementation means the behavior you measured historically is the behavior you deploy, which massively reduces surprises and debugging time.

How: make the strategy depend only on abstract interfaces — an event source and an order interface — not on concrete feeds or gateways. Swap the event source (historical file → simulator → live multicast) and the order sink (simulated matcher → paper account → live exchange gateway) without touching strategy code. Drive timers from the same event clock. The only differences between modes are at the edges (I/O and a realistic fill model in simulation), so the decision logic is identical everywhere.

interviewQuestions.q: Why do many HFT strategy engines run single-threaded, and isn't that leaving performance on the table?
a: A single-threaded event loop processes one ordered stream of events (market + own-order + timers) through deterministic callbacks, with no shared mutable state between threads. The benefits are large: no locks or atomics on the hot path (no contention, no synchronization latency), no data races, and — crucially — fully reproducible behavior given the same event sequence, which makes debugging, replay, and backtest=live parity possible. It's also often *faster* per event because there's zero synchronization overhead and the working set stays hot in one core's cache.

It's not really leaving performance on the table, because the parallelism in a trading system is across *stages* (feed handler, book, strategy, OMS each on their own pinned core, connected by lock-free rings or a Disruptor) and across *instruments/strategies* (shard by symbol to different cores), not within a single strategy's decision loop. Trying to multi-thread one strategy's state would add locking/coordination that usually costs more latency and determinism than it gains. So the pattern is: single-threaded, deterministic engine per shard, with parallelism achieved by pipelining stages and sharding instruments — keeping each hot loop lock-free and reproducible.
followups: How would you scale to thousands of instruments?
How does single-threading enable backtest=live parity?

problems.title: Design an event-driven market-making engine
problems.statement: Design the strategy engine for a single-instrument market maker. Specify the event types it handles, the per-event work (kept fast/deterministic), the state it maintains, how research parameters get in without disturbing the hot path, and how the same engine runs in backtest and live. Call out the own-order edge cases you must handle.
problems.hint: Single-threaded merged event loop; precomputed ParamSet swapped atomically; compact O(1) state; abstract event source + order sink; handle partial fills / fill-before-ack / rejects.

approach: Events: market-data book updates and trades, own-order lifecycle (ack, fill/partial-fill, cancel-ack, reject), and timers — all merged into one time-ordered stream processed by a single thread (no locks, reproducible). Per event: onBookUpdate computes microprice + inventory skew from the current ParamSet and re-quotes by diffing desired vs resting orders (only send changes / modifies); onFill updates inventory and PnL and may hedge or re-quote; onTimer refreshes/ages quotes; onReject backs off and re-evaluates. Each handler is a small arithmetic+comparison routine that enqueues order actions to the OMS over a lock-free ring — no allocation on the path.

State (compact, cache-resident, O(1) updates): working orders keyed by id with their price level and estimated queue position; inventory and average price; realized/unrealized PnL; active timers; and the current ParamSet. Research runs offline/side-thread and publishes a new ParamSet via an atomic double-buffer pointer the hot path reads without locking.

Backtest = live: the engine depends only on an EventSource and an OrderSink interface. In backtest, the source is a historical/simulated feed and the sink is a realistic fill simulator (queue-position-aware, with latency); in live, the source is the multicast feed/book and the sink is the exchange gateway. The strategy code is identical; only the edges differ.

Own-order edge cases to handle: partial fills (reduce remaining qty, keep the order), a fill arriving before its ack (reconcile by id), rejects (from pre-trade risk or the exchange — don't assume the order rests), cancel-reject (the order may have just filled), and out-of-order acks. Mishandling these is the top source of live bugs, so model them explicitly and replay recorded sequences to test.

problems.title: Handle own-order races correctly
problems.statement: Your market-making engine sends a buy order, then a cancel for it. Design how the engine's state machine handles these out-of-order/edge sequences correctly: (a) a fill arrives before the order's ack; (b) the order partially fills, then your cancel is acked for the remainder; (c) you send a cancel but get a cancel-reject because it already fully filled; (d) two partial fills arrive out of order. Why are these the top source of live bugs?
problems.hint: Key everything by client order id; track leaves/filled; treat the exchange's execution reports as ground truth; cancel-reject often means 'already filled'.

approach: Model each order by a unique client order id with explicit state and quantities (ordered, filled, leaves) and treat the exchange's execution reports as ground truth, reconciling by id. (a) Fill-before-ack: apply the fill by id (reduce leaves, update inventory/P&L) even though you haven't seen the ack yet — the fill proves the order is live; when the ack arrives, don't double-count, just confirm the order rests/rested. (b) Partial fill then cancel-ack-for-remainder: reduce leaves on the partial; the cancel-ack tells you the *remaining* leaves are cancelled, so set leaves=0 and the order terminal — never assume the cancel removed the already-filled portion. (c) Cancel-reject because already filled: interpret 'too late to cancel' as the order having fully filled (or otherwise terminal); trust the fills/drop-copy, mark the order filled, and update inventory — do not assume it's still working. (d) Out-of-order partial fills: dedupe by execution id and apply each once; track cumulative filled and recompute leaves from cumulative quantities rather than assuming arrival order, so reordering/duplication can't corrupt the position.

General principle: the engine's view of position and working orders must be driven by reconciling exchange messages (acks/fills/cancels/rejects) by id and execution id, idempotently, with the exchange (and drop-copy) as the source of truth — never by optimistic local assumptions about message order.

Why these are the top source of live bugs: they're rare, timing-dependent edge cases that don't occur in simple backtests or happy-path testing, but happen constantly in production under load (the network and matching engine don't guarantee your assumed ordering). Mishandling them causes phantom positions, double-counted fills, 'I thought I cancelled that', and risk-limit breaches — real money lost. That's why robust engines model these explicitly and test them by replaying recorded adversarial message sequences.
